name: Tera
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Newman, Paul. 1970. A Grammar of Tera. UC Press. On archive.org but lending-restricted (search-inside blocked); Rosetta excerpt read is a phoneme chart with no stress/tone statement.

new_statements.quote: The tone system of Tera has not been described before. What follows is a preliminary analysis of mono- and disyllabic lexical items; no attempt has yet been made to investigate tone in discourse. [...] There are three contrasting level tones: high (H [´]), mid (M, unmarked) and low (L [`]). There appear to be no contour tones, even in syllables with long and diphthongal vowels. [...] Disyllabic words display the following seven patterns; there appear to be no sequences of HL or LH. || Newman 1964:35: "Tera has three basic tones: high ´, mid (unmarked in this paper) and low `. What appear as rising and falling tones can in all cases be analysed as a sequence of two level tones."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tera is described as a lexical tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) on every syllable; neither Tench 2007 nor Newman 1964 says anything about word stress or accent, so no stress placement rule is on record in the accessible primary descriptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone notes only: no HL/LH on disyllables; mid tone partially assimilates to neighbouring H or L; possible voicing-tone interaction (voiced obstruents favour L).
new_statements.domain_note: Both descriptions treat isolated lexical items (mono- and disyllables); Tench explicitly has not analysed tone in discourse, Newman fn.7 likewise for longer utterances. Silence on stress is silence, not a claim that stress is absent.
new_statements.identity_note: Tench 2007 describes the 'standard' Tera of radio news, from speakers of Deba, Hinna, Difa, Zambuk and Lubo (Gombe State); Newman 1964/1970 are based on one speaker from Wuyo (eastern Tera area). Same language, tera1251; Newman notes Tera and Pidlimdi (Hinna) form one dialect cluster.

sources.note: Nothing. Phonology pp.34-35: consonants, six vowels + six diphthongs ('each diphthong... carries a single level tone'), vowel length not phonemic, sec.4 'Tera has three basic tones: high, mid, low'; fn.7 'Three tonemes are necessary and sufficient for marking lexical items.' No mention of stress or accent.
